_strings.@@3784d2a288d5: Property Tax Deduction/Credit (homeowners and renters) — Residents who were domiciled in NJ and maintained a primary residence as a homeowner or tenant during 2023 that was subject to property taxes (paid directly as a homeowner, or through rent for tenants). Taxpayer chooses EITHER the deduction OR the credit (whichever is more beneficial). For tenants, the residence must have a separate kitchen and bath. The credit (vs. deduction) is generally taken by those age 65+, blind/disabled, or whose income is below the filing threshold. 18% of rent paid during the year is treated as property taxes paid.
_strings.@@42581db63846: Child and Dependent Care Credit — Resident taxpayers who have earned income, paid someone to care for one or more qualifying persons (a child under 13 or a dependent/spouse incapable of self-care) so they could work or look for work, and who were allowed the federal child and dependent care credit. Married filing separately generally not eligible unless federal exceptions are met. Civil union and non-joint-federal filers follow special worksheet rules.

The dependent must be claimed on Lines 10/11 of the NJ-1040. Married filing separately is not eligible. The per-child credit was increased for Tax Year 2023.

_strings.@@a4a988f695a7: Treaty conformity — NJ does NOT conform to federal tax treaties: income exempt from federal tax under a treaty is STILL taxable by NJ. Do not carry a federal treaty exclusion onto the state return. (This is about TREATY conformity only — a state's Internal Revenue Code conformity date and its deduction/credit conformity are separate questions; see any law-change lines below.) State note: New Jersey does NOT start from federal AGI. The NJ Gross Income Tax is a self-contained system that builds gross income from its own statutory categories. The 2023 NJ-1040 instructions explicitly direct: "Use 'State Wages' from box 16 of your W-2, not federal wages (box 1)" and warn that "State wages (box 16) [can be] higher than your federal wages (box 1)," and that if income taxable for NJ is not in box 16 you "must add that amount back into your State wages." Because NJ never imports federal AGI, a federal tax-treaty exemption (which reduces federal box 1 / federal AGI) does NOT automatically pass through. NJ's Gross Income Tax Act contains no provision recognizing federal income tax treaties, so federally treaty-exempt wages are generally still taxable for NJ purposes. This puts NJ in the "builds income from scratch, no treaty pass-through" category -> conforms_to_federal_treaties = false. (Conservative reading; the precise NJ treatment of a specific treaty article should be confirmed at the DOR.)
_strings.@@b187e320fc64: New Jersey Earned Income Tax Credit (NJEITC) — New Jersey residents who work and have earned income and who claimed and were allowed the federal Earned Income Credit (EIC). Residents at least 18 years old (with or without a qualifying child) may apply even if they did not meet the federal age requirement; must meet federal EIC income limits and have a valid SSN. Claimed by filing Form NJ-1040.

NJ never starts from federal AGI — gross income is built from NJ's own categories (wages from W-2 box 16 State wages). The op subtracts $1,000 x exemptions_count (Line 6 regular exemptions: self, spouse/CU partner, or registered domestic partner) and $1,500 x dependents_count (Line 10 qualified dependent children plus Line 11 other dependents) to approximate Line 42 New Jersey Taxable Income. If any UNMODELED subtraction applies — Line 7 senior 65+ ($1,000 each), Line 8 blind/disabled ($1,000 each), Line 9 veteran ($6,000 each), Line 12 dependent attending college ($1,000 each), Lines 31-37c deductions (medical over 2% of gross income, alimony, qualified conservation, health enterprise zone, alternative business calculation, organ/bone marrow donation, NJBEST up to $10,000, NJCLASS up to $2,500, tuition up to $10,000), or the Line 41 Property Tax Deduction (up to $15,000; $7,500 MFS same home) — reduce the supplied base by those amounts too, or compute on the form; otherwise the result will overstate Line 43. Tax Table MANDATE below $100,000: Line 43 directs 'If the income on line 42 is less than $100,000, use the Tax Table on page 54. Otherwise, calculate the tax by using the Tax Rate Schedules on page 63.' Bracket math may differ by a few dollars within table bands; the filed form must use the table below $100,000. The Tax Rate Schedules (shipped here) govern at $100,000 and above. Filing threshold = no tax due: you are not required to file (and owe no NJ tax) if New Jersey gross income (Line 29) is at or below $10,000 (single; married/CU partner filing separate) or $20,000 (married/CU couple filing joint; head of household; qualifying widow(er)/surviving CU partner). NOT modeled — the brackets tax from the first dollar, so below-threshold filers would be overstated; file only to recover withholding or refundable credits. Printed-constant divergence (Table B only): the 70,000-80,000 bracket prints 'multiply by .035, subtract $1,154.50', but the exact cumulative constant is $1,155.00 — the printed schedule yields $0.50 MORE than exact marginal-bracket math everywhere inside that bracket, and rejoins exactly at $80,000 (the next constant, $2,775.00, is exact). Every other printed constant in Tables A and B equals the cumulative sum exactly. One schedule covers three statuses: Table B applies identically to married/CU couple filing joint, head of household, and qualifying widow(er)/surviving CU partner — the head_of_household brackets shipped here are Table B, identical to married_filing_jointly, and the engine's QSS->married_filing_jointly mapping is exact (no divergence). Table A applies to single and married/CU partner filing separate (MFS is NOT half of MFJ; copied as printed). Civil-union partners must use the corresponding married/CU filing statuses. New Jersey has NO standard deduction — standard_deduction is null because none exists, not because it is income-dependent. NJ instead allows specific deductions on Lines 31-37c (medical expenses over 2% of gross income, alimony, qualified conservation contribution, health enterprise zone, alternative business calculation adjustment, organ/bone marrow donation, up to $10,000 NJBEST 529 contributions, up to $2,500 NJCLASS loan principal and interest, up to $10,000 tuition) and the Line 41 Property Tax Deduction (property taxes paid or 18% of rent, capped at $15,000; $7,500 if married filing separately sharing the same main home). None of these are modeled. The op applies ONLY the $1,000 Line 6 regular exemption (x exemptions_count) and the $1,500 Line 10/11 dependent exemption (x dependents_count). The result equals Form NJ-1040 Line 43 only when no other exemption (senior, blind/disabled, veteran, college dependent) and no Lines 31-37c or Line 41 deduction applies; otherwise pre-subtract those amounts from the base you supply. NJ exemptions are genuine BASE reductions (Line 13 total -> Line 30, subtracted from gross income before the rates), not credits. Separately, NJ's refundable CREDITS are not modeled: NJ Earned Income Tax Credit (Line 58, 40% of federal EIC), $50 Property Tax Credit (Line 56), Child and Dependent Care Credit (Line 64), NJ Child Tax Credit (Line 65, up to $1,000 per child age 5 or younger), and the Credit for Income Taxes Paid to Other Jurisdictions (Line 44). Part-year residents must prorate the Line 13 exemption total on Line 30 by months of NJ residency (15+ days counts as a month) — NOT modeled; full-year exemption amounts are shipped. No 2023 rate change: the 2023 schedules (top rate 10.75% over $1,000,000) are the final published schedules used for the 2023 filing season; New Jersey had no mid-year retroactive rate legislation for 2023.
